title: Demystifying the Scribes behind the Voynich Manuscript using Computational Linguistic Techniques
authors: Kevin Farrugia, Colin Layfield, Lonneke van der Plas
summary: The authors train character n-gram classifiers to predict Davis's palaeographic page labels, using page-level cross-validation. The comparison uses the proposed labels as training data and includes only three of the five proposed hands; agreement with those labels is not a direct independent count of scribes.
established: The Zandbergen version 1r EVA text was balanced to 31 pages for each of hands 1, 2 and 3; hands 4 and 5 were excluded for limited data. The balanced classes differed substantially in word count: 4,660, 9,241 and 10,698 respectively (section 3.1, Tables 1–2).

Four classifiers used character bigram and trigram features in separate ten-fold page-level cross-validation runs, with feature extraction after splitting. Reported accuracies ranged from 73.1% to 90.3% with trigrams and 65.6% to 84.9% with bigrams (sections 3.2 and 4, Table 4).

All four trigram classifiers agreed with each other but disagreed with the palaeographic labels on seven pages: f57v, f65v, f85r, f86v, f95r, f95v and f116v. The paper notes that low word counts remain a limitation for some pages (section 4).

The decision-tree root features ed and edy match a known Currier A/B distinction, and the authors note confusion between hands 2 and 3; their task predicts the existing hand labels and does not measure new handwriting features (section 4).

open.question: What do independent palaeographic and stylometric checks show for the pages where all four trigram classifiers disagreed with the original hand assignments?
open.check: Predefine a blind image-feature assessment and compare the seven reported pages with matched pages from the candidate hands, without using the classifier predictions to label the images.
